mainTopic: רב's rule about a גוי in a מבוי and a חצר, and the משנה of two courtyards one inside the other, with the three-way dispute over whether a resident's right of passage forbids
overview: This amud opens by finishing a צריכותא: רב needed two rulings, one teaching that a גוי's home is not a real דירה and one teaching that a מבוי needs two houses. Because רב applied his rule even to a חצר, the גמרא concludes his reason is אסור לעשות יחיד במקום גוי, and רב יוסף says this explains why רבי טבלא said 'גוי, גוי' twice. Then a new משנה describes two courtyards, one inside the other, and rules who forbids whom when one or both made an עירוב, when someone forgot to join, and when they share one עירוב. רבי עקיבא holds that the inner residents' דריסת הרגל forbids the outer courtyard, and the חכמים disagree. In the גמרא, רב דימי reports that רבי ינאי assigned a clause to רבי עקיבא and said the חכמים hold that no 'foot' forbids. The גמרא challenges this again and again from the משנה, which seems to assume a middle view: a permitted foot does not forbid, but a forbidden foot does. Finally רבין gives a corrected version: the תנא קמא holds the middle view, רבי עקיבא is the strictest, and the later רבנן are the most lenient. The amud closes by explaining that 'one place' in the משנה means the outer courtyard, a place designated for both.

steps.title: Why the first ruling alone was not enough
steps.stepSummary: If רב had only said the general rule about how many houses a מבוי needs, we might have counted a גוי's home as a home. So he had to teach that a גוי's residence does not count.
steps.simpleTranslation: I would have said that a גוי's residence counts as a residence. So he teaches us that a גוי's residence does not count as a residence.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is explaining why רב needed his ruling about the גוי. Without it, we would have wrongly counted a גוי's house toward the houses a מבוי needs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב gave a general rule that a מבוי needs a certain number of houses and courtyards opening into it. From that rule alone, you might think any house counts, including one where a גוי lives. His separate ruling fixes this: for these laws, דירת גוי is not a real דירה.

keyTerms.meaning: I would have thought (the mistaken first assumption)
the residence of a non-Jew
it is legally called a residence
he teaches us (the new point being made)

steps.confusionAlert: We are starting in the middle of the argument. Earlier, the גמרא quoted two rulings of רב and asked why both were needed. This line is the first half of the answer.

phrases.english: I would have said:
a gentile's residence is considered a residence,
phrases.notes: So it would count toward the houses that a מבוי needs.

phrases.english: so he teaches us
that a gentile's residence is not considered a residence.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲוָה אָמֵינָא: דִּירַת גּוֹי שְׁמָהּ דִּירָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the צריכותא on the previous amud, which asked why רב needed two rulings.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: showing that each ruling teaches something the other cannot
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A גוי's home counts as a home for the laws of a מבוי.
steps.terutzMaskana: A גוי's home does not count, so the ruling about the גוי is needed.

steps.title: Why the ruling about the גוי alone was not enough
steps.stepSummary: If רב had only given the ruling about the גוי, we would not know how many houses a מבוי needs. So he also had to teach that it needs two houses.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he had taught only from here, I would have said: I don't know how many houses are needed. So he teaches us: two houses.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the second half of the answer. Now the גמרא shows why the general ruling was also necessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling about the גוי tells us that his house does not count. It does not tell us the minimum number of houses that do count. The general ruling fills in that number: two houses. Each ruling therefore teaches something the other does not.

keyTerms.meaning: and if only from here (if we had only this source)
I would not know
two houses

steps.whatToRemember: Both of רב's rulings are needed. One teaches that a גוי's home does not count. The other teaches that a מבוי needs at least two (Jewish) houses.

phrases.english: And if only from here —
phrases.notes: Meaning, if רב had given only his ruling about the גוי.

phrases.english: I would have said:
I do not know how many houses are needed,
so he teaches us: two houses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the two-sided צריכותא begun in step 1.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: From the ruling about the גוי alone, the minimum number of houses would be unknown.
steps.terutzMaskana: The general ruling sets the minimum at two houses.

steps.title: The real reason behind רב's rule
steps.stepSummary: Since רב applied his rule even to a חצר, his reason must be that a Jew should not live alone in a place where a גוי lives.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that רב said this applies even to a courtyard, the reason for רב's view is that he holds: it is forbidden to set up a lone Jew in the place of a גוי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא looks at how far רב stretched his rule and uses that to work out his underlying reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, a single Jew in a חצר may carry there freely, so the problem is not the house count. If רב forbids it even in a חצר, his reason must be different. He holds אסור לעשות יחיד במקום גוי: the חכמים made life harder for a Jew who lives alone among non-Jews, so that he will move away.

keyTerms.meaning: now (that we know this)
the reason
because he holds
it is forbidden for an individual Jew to settle alone where a non-Jew lives

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that רב's rule about a גוי is not only a technical counting rule. It is a rabbinic policy meant to discourage a Jew from living alone among non-Jews.

phrases.english: Now that Rav said it applies even to a courtyard,
the reason of Rav is that he holds
it is forbidden to establish an individual in the place of a gentile.
phrases.notes: The חכמים did not let him make his carrying easier, so that he would move away.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on רב's rulings to identify the reasoning behind them.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב's reason is the policy of אסור לעשות יחיד במקום גוי.

steps.title: רב יוסף finally understands רבי טבלא
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף says this explains why he once heard רבי טבלא say "גוי, גוי" twice. He had not understood it until now.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: If so, this is why I heard רבי טבלא say "גוי, גוי" two times, and I did not know what he meant.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף offers support from a teaching he remembered. It now makes sense in light of the two cases, the מבוי and the חצר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי טבלא said "גוי" twice, and רב יוסף could not tell why. Now that we know רב's rule about a גוי applies in two settings, a מבוי and a חצר, the double mention fits. Each "גוי" refers to one of the two cases.

keyTerms.meaning: if so
this is (what explains)
רבי טבלא, a student of רב
two times

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
If so, this explains
why I heard Rabbi Tavla
say: "A gentile, a gentile" two times,
phrases.notes: One mention for the מבוי and one for the חצר.

phrases.english: and I did not know what he was saying.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: אִי הָכִי הַיְינוּ דִּשְׁמַעְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the conclusion that רב's rule about a גוי applies in two settings.
steps.raayaObject: That רב's rule applies to both a מבוי and a חצר

steps.title: New משנה: two courtyards, one inside the other
steps.stepSummary: There are two courtyards, one inside the other. If only the inner one made an עירוב, carrying is permitted in the inner one and forbidden in the outer one.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Two courtyards, one inside the other. If the inner one made an עירוב and the outer one did not, the inner one is permitted and the outer one is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It describes an inner courtyard whose only exit passes through an outer courtyard, where only the inner courtyard made an עירוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The people of the inner courtyard walk through the outer courtyard, so they have a דריסת הרגל (right of passage) there. That right does not hurt the inner courtyard. Its residents made their own עירוב, so they may carry there. The outer courtyard made no עירוב, so carrying there stays forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: our משנה
one inside the other
made an עירוב
the inner one
the outer one

steps.confusionAlert: "Inside the other" means the inner courtyard has no exit of its own to the street. Its residents must pass through the outer courtyard.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
Two courtyards, one inside the other,
the inner one made an eiruv
and the outer one did not make an eiruv —
the inner one is permitted
and the outer one is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ שְׁתֵּי חֲצֵירוֹת זוֹ לִפְנִים מִזּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה and a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If only the inner courtyard made an עירוב, carrying is permitted in the inner courtyard and forbidden in the outer courtyard.

steps.title: Only the outer courtyard made an עירוב: both are forbidden
steps.stepSummary: If the חיצונה made an עירוב and the פנימית did not, carrying is forbidden in both courtyards.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the outer courtyard made an עירוב but the inner one did not, carrying is forbidden in both.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the opposite case of Step 5: now only the outer courtyard made an עירוב, and the result is that both courtyards are forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The inner courtyard is forbidden simply because it made no עירוב. The outer courtyard is also forbidden, even though it made an עירוב. The inner residents walk through it, so they count like residents who did not join the outer courtyard's עירוב.

keyTerms.meaning: The outer courtyard, which opens to the street
The inner courtyard, whose residents must pass through the outer one
Both of them are forbidden for carrying

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the outer courtyard's own עירוב is enough. The inner residents' right to walk through it means they count as 'neighbors' who did not join, and that ruins the outer courtyard's עירוב.

phrases.english: If the outer one made an eruv and not the inner one —
phrases.notes: The verb עירבה (made an עירוב) carries over from Step 5.

phrases.english: both are forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reverses the case of Step 5. There only the inner courtyard made an עירוב; here only the outer one did.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When only the outer courtyard makes an עירוב, carrying is forbidden in both courtyards.

steps.title: Each courtyard made its own separate עירוב
steps.stepSummary: If each courtyard made its own separate עירוב, each one is permitted on its own.
steps.simpleTranslation: If this courtyard made an עירוב for itself and that courtyard made an עירוב for itself, each one is permitted on its own.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the case where both courtyards made separate עירובין, and each one may carry inside itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each courtyard is now organized internally, so carrying within each is allowed. Since they did not make a joint עירוב, carrying from one courtyard into the other is still not allowed. רבי עקיבא disagrees in the next step. The גמרא later assigns this ruling to the תנא קמא (Step 23).

keyTerms.meaning: For itself, on its own
By itself, separately
Permitted (for carrying)

phrases.english: If this one made an eruv for itself
and that one for itself —
this one is permitted by itself
and that one is permitted by itself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from cases where only one courtyard made an עירוב to the case where each made its own.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two separate עירובין allow carrying within each courtyard, but not between them.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: the right of way forbids the outer courtyard
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא disagrees with Step 7. He says the outer courtyard stays forbidden because of the inner residents' דריסת הרגל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא forbids carrying in the outer courtyard, because the right of passage of the inner residents makes it forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא argues on the last case: even when each courtyard made its own עירוב, he says the outer courtyard is still forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי עקיבא, simply having the right to walk through a courtyard gives the inner residents enough of a share in it to forbid it. This holds even though they made their own עירוב. Their foothold in the outer courtyard was never included in the outer courtyard's עירוב.

keyTerms.meaning: The תנא who holds the stricter view here
Literally 'treading of the foot': the right to walk through someone else's area
It makes it forbidden

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva forbids the outer one,
because the right of passage makes it forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the ruling of Step 7 about the outer courtyard.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דריסת הרגל alone is enough to forbid the outer courtyard, even when each courtyard made its own עירוב.

steps.title: The חכמים: the right of way does not forbid
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים answer that דריסת הרגל alone does not forbid the outer courtyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים say: the right of passage does not make it forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים give the opposite view to רבי עקיבא, so the ruling of Step 7 stands: each courtyard is permitted on its own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The inner residents only pass through the outer courtyard, and they already carry freely in their own courtyard. So the חכמים hold that this limited right of passage is not a real enough presence to block the outer courtyard's עירוב.

keyTerms.meaning: The majority of the Sages
It does not

steps.whyThisMatters: Under the גמרא's final reading (רבין's version in Step 23), these חכמים are the most lenient opinion: the right of passage never forbids the outer courtyard, even when the inner residents made no עירוב. The strict rulings in Steps 6 and 11 belong to the תנא קמא, not to these חכמים.

phrases.english: And the Sages say:
the right of passage does not make it forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly disputes רבי עקיבא's reasoning in Step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דריסת הרגל by itself does not forbid the outer courtyard when the inner courtyard has its own עירוב.

steps.title: Someone from the outer courtyard forgot to join
steps.stepSummary: If one person in the outer courtyard forgot to join the עירוב, the inner courtyard is permitted and the outer is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: If one person from the outer courtyard forgot and did not join the עירוב, the inner courtyard is permitted and the outer one is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now looks at what happens when one resident forgets to join. This first case is a forgetter in the outer courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The forgetter lives in the outer courtyard and has no right to walk through the inner one. So he forbids only his own courtyard, and the problem does not spread inward.

keyTerms.meaning: He forgot
And did not join the עירוב

phrases.english: If one person from the outer one forgot
and did not join the eruv —
the inner one is permitted
and the outer one is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁכַח אֶחָד מִן הַחִיצוֹנָה וְלֹא עֵירַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the רבי עקיבא and חכמים dispute to cases where an individual forgot to join.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A forgetter in the outer courtyard forbids only the outer courtyard.

steps.title: Someone from the inner courtyard forgot to join
steps.stepSummary: If the forgetter is from the inner courtyard, both courtyards are forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: If one person from the inner courtyard forgot and did not join the עירוב, both courtyards are forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the matching case: now the forgetter lives in the inner courtyard, and the result is stricter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The forgetter forbids his own inner courtyard. He also has the right to walk through the outer courtyard, so he forbids that one too. A problem in the inner courtyard spreads outward, but a problem in the outer courtyard does not spread inward.

keyTerms.meaning: From the inner courtyard

steps.whatToRemember: Rule of direction: the inner courtyard can affect the outer one, because its residents pass through it. The outer courtyard never affects the inner one.

phrases.english: If from the inner one, and he did not join the eruv —
both are forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The matching case to Step 10, with the forgetter in the inner courtyard instead of the outer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A forgetter in the inner courtyard forbids both courtyards.

steps.title: One shared עירוב and someone forgot
steps.stepSummary: If both courtyards put their עירוב in one place and anyone forgot to join, from either courtyard, both are forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: If they placed their עירוב in one place and one person forgot, whether from the inner or the outer courtyard, and did not join, both courtyards are forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now gives the case of one joint עירוב shared by both courtyards, where one person from either courtyard forgot to join.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A shared עירוב turns the two courtyards into one unit. So it no longer matters which side the forgetter lives on: one missing person ruins the whole joint עירוב. This differs from Step 10, where a forgetter in the outer courtyard did not affect the inner one.

keyTerms.meaning: They placed their עירוב
In one place, meaning one joint עירוב for both courtyards
Whether ... or

phrases.english: If they placed their eruv in one place
and one person forgot,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין מִן הַפְּנִימִית בֵּין מִן הַחִיצוֹנָה,
phrases.english: whether from the inner one or from the outer one,
and did not join the eruv —
both are forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts with Steps 10 and 11. There each courtyard had its own עירוב; here they share one.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: With a joint עירוב, anyone from either courtyard who fails to join forbids both courtyards.

steps.title: Courtyards with only one resident need no עירוב
steps.stepSummary: If each courtyard has only a single resident, no עירוב is needed at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the courtyards belonged to single individuals, they do not need to make an עירוב.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה closes with a limit on all the cases above: everything said applies only when courtyards have several residents.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An עירוב is needed to join many owners into one shared household. When one person lives alone in each courtyard, there is no one to join with, so he may carry freely. This holds even though the inner resident passes through the outer courtyard.

keyTerms.meaning: Single individuals, one resident per courtyard
They do not need to make an עירוב

steps.whatToRemember: All the rules of this משנה (who forbids whom) apply only when several residents share a courtyard. A courtyard with a single resident needs no עירוב.

phrases.english: And if they belonged to individuals —
they do not need to make an eruv.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits all the earlier cases to courtyards that have several residents.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Courtyards with one resident each require no עירוב.

steps.title: רבי ינאי says the case in the משנה follows רבי עקיבא
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי reports in the name of רבי ינאי that the clause 'the outer made an עירוב, the inner did not, both are forbidden' follows רבי עקיבא, who holds that even a permitted foot forbids. The חכמים say neither a permitted foot nor a forbidden foot forbids.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב דימי came from ארץ ישראל, he said in the name of רבי ינאי: this part of the משנה follows רבי עקיבא. He holds that even a 'foot' that is permitted in its own courtyard still makes another courtyard forbidden. But the חכמים say: just as a permitted foot does not forbid, a forbidden foot also does not forbid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens by telling us whose opinion the משנה's case follows. רבי ינאי says the case of 'outer made an עירוב, inner did not, both forbidden' follows רבי עקיבא, not the חכמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'foot' means the inner residents' right to walk through the outer courtyard (דריסת הרגל). רבי עקיבא says this walking right forbids the outer courtyard even when the inner residents are permitted at home, so it certainly forbids when they are not. The חכמים say the walking right never forbids the outer courtyard, so in this case they would permit the outer courtyard.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה
When רב דימי came (from ארץ ישראל to בבל, bringing teachings)
A 'foot' permitted in its own place: residents who may carry in their own courtyard
Not in its own place: the other courtyard they pass through
A 'forbidden foot': residents who may not carry in their own courtyard because they made no עירוב

steps.whyThisMatters: The rest of this section tests whether רבי ינאי's claim fits the wording of the משנה.

phrases.english: Gemara
When Rav Dimi came
he said in the name of Rabbi Yannai:
This is the statement of Rabbi Akiva,
who said: even a foot that is permitted in its own place
forbids when it is not in its own place.
But the Rabbis say:
Just as a permitted foot does not forbid,
so too a forbidden foot does not forbid.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי אָמַר רַבִּי יַנַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: First גמרא statement on the משנה. It assigns the case of 'outer made an עירוב, inner did not' to רבי עקיבא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The clause 'outer made an עירוב and inner did not, both forbidden' follows רבי עקיבא. The חכמים hold that neither a permitted foot nor a forbidden foot forbids another courtyard.

steps.title: If it were רבי עקיבא, why mention a forbidden foot?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי ינאי. According to רבי עקיבא, even a permitted foot forbids, so the משנה should not need the case where the inner courtyard made no עירוב. That suggests the case follows the חכמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: if the outer courtyard made an עירוב and the inner did not, both are forbidden. Whose opinion is this? If you say רבי עקיבא, why speak specifically about a forbidden foot? For him, even a permitted foot also forbids. So isn't it the חכמים?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי ינאי's claim. It argues that the משנה's specific case makes more sense according to the חכמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי עקיבא, the outer courtyard is forbidden even if the inner courtyard did make an עירוב. So mentioning 'the inner did not' seems pointless for him. If the case follows the חכמים, then the חכמים hold that a forbidden foot does forbid, which contradicts רבי ינאי's report of their view.

keyTerms.meaning: We learned (in the משנה)
Whose opinion is this?
If you say
Why specifically this case?
Rather, is it not...? (pushing toward the other option)

phrases.english: We learned:
If the outer one made an eiruv and the inner one did not,
both are forbidden.
Whose opinion is this?
If you say it is Rabbi Akiva,
why specifically a forbidden foot?
Even a permitted foot also forbids.
Rather, is it not the Rabbis?!

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנַן עֵירְבָה חִיצוֹנָה וְלֹא פְּנִימִית שְׁתֵּיהֶן אֲסוּרוֹת מַנִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי ינאי's attribution in step 14, using the משנה's wording.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ינאי's claim that the clause follows רבי עקיבא and that the חכמים hold a forbidden foot does not forbid.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: For רבי עקיבא, mentioning a forbidden foot is unnecessary, since a permitted foot already forbids. So the clause must be the חכמים, who would then hold that a forbidden foot forbids.

steps.title: It is רבי עקיבא, teaching the smaller case before the bigger one
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the clause really is רבי עקיבא. The משנה uses a 'not only this, but even that' style: it teaches the simpler case first, then the bigger one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, it is רבי עקיבא. The משנה teaches in a 'not only this, but even that' style.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבי ינאי. It explains why רבי עקיבא's משנה would still mention the forbidden-foot case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה first teaches the easy case: when the inner courtyard made no עירוב, the outer is forbidden. Then it adds the bigger new idea: even when each courtyard made its own עירוב, רבי עקיבא forbids the outer courtyard. So mentioning the easy case first proves nothing about whose opinion it is.

keyTerms.meaning: Really / actually (holding on to the original position)
'Not only this, but even that': teaching a simpler case and then a bigger one
It (the משנה) teaches

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the simpler case is pointless because a bigger case comes later. 'לא זו אף זו' is a recognized teaching style: the משנה deliberately builds from the easy case to the bigger one.

phrases.english: Actually, it is Rabbi Akiva,
and it teaches in the style of 'not only this, but even that.'

steps.triggerLanguage: לְעוֹלָם רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא וְלֹא זוֹ אַף זוֹ קָתָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 15 and keeps רבי ינאי's attribution.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the משנה's teaching style (לא זו אף זו)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Mentioning a forbidden foot means the clause cannot be רבי עקיבא's.
steps.terutzMaskana: The clause is רבי עקיבא's. The משנה teaches the simpler case first and then the bigger one, where each courtyard made its own עירוב.

steps.title: Setting up a second challenge from the case where each courtyard made its own עירוב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case where each courtyard made its own עירוב and both are permitted. It infers that if the inner courtyard had not made an עירוב, both would be forbidden. This inference is being prepared as a new challenge to רבי ינאי.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: if this courtyard made an עירוב for itself and that one made an עירוב for itself, each is permitted on its own. The reason is that they made an עירוב. But if the inner one did not make an עירוב, both would be forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It reads a later case in the משנה closely and draws an inference that will be used against רבי ינאי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying both courtyards are permitted in this case does not fit רבי עקיבא, who forbids the outer courtyard even here. So this part looks like the חכמים. The inference 'if the inner did not make an עירוב, both are forbidden' would then mean the חכמים hold that a forbidden foot does forbid, against what רבי ינאי reported. Step 18 completes this challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: This courtyard made an עירוב for itself (separately)
By itself: permitted within its own courtyard only
The reason is...
But (by inference) if not...

phrases.english: We learned: if this one made an eiruv for itself
and that one for itself,
this one is permitted by itself
and that one is permitted by itself.
The reason is that it made an eiruv;
but if it did not make an eiruv,
both would be forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנַן עֵירְבָה זוֹ לְעַצְמָהּ וְזוֹ לְעַצְמָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending רבי ינאי in step 16, the גמרא opens a second challenge using an inference from a later case in the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ינאי's report that the חכמים hold a forbidden foot does not forbid.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The case where each courtyard made its own עירוב and both are permitted seems to be the חכמים. Its inference, that without the inner courtyard's עירוב both are forbidden, would mean the חכמים hold that a forbidden foot forbids the outer courtyard.

steps.title: Who holds that only a forbidden foot forbids?
steps.stepSummary: The inference from the משנה matches a view where a permitted foot does not forbid but a forbidden foot does. That cannot be רבי עקיבא, so it must be the חכמים, which contradicts רבי ינאי.
steps.simpleTranslation: But this תנא, who says a permitted foot does not forbid and a forbidden foot does forbid, who is he? If you say he is רבי עקיבא, that cannot be, because רבי עקיבא holds that even a permitted foot forbids. So isn't it the חכמים?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the challenge it set up in step 17. It asks who could be the author of the inference it just drew from the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה quoted in step 17 states that when each courtyard made its own עירוב, both courtyards are permitted. That means a permitted foot does not forbid. Step 17 then inferred that without the inner courtyard's עירוב, both are forbidden, meaning a forbidden foot does forbid. רבי עקיבא holds that even a permitted foot forbids, so this view must belong to the חכמים. That would mean the חכמים agree a forbidden foot does forbid, which goes against רבי ינאי's claim that for them neither foot forbids.

keyTerms.meaning: A 'permitted foot': residents of the inner courtyard who may carry in their own courtyard.
A 'forbidden foot': residents of the inner courtyard who may not carry in their own courtyard.
Who is the author?
If you say
Rather, is it not that

phrases.english: But this tanna, who said:
a permitted foot does not forbid
a forbidden foot does forbid,
who is this?
If you say it is Rabbi Akiva —
but for him even a permitted foot also forbids,
phrases.notes: רבי עקיבא holds that any right of passage forbids.

phrases.english: rather, is it not the Rabbis?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge that step 17 set up.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ינאי's claim that the חכמים hold neither a permitted nor a forbidden foot forbids.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה implies a permitted foot does not forbid. רבי עקיבא cannot hold that, so the view must be the חכמים. The same clause shows a forbidden foot does forbid, so the חכמים must agree a forbidden foot forbids.

steps.title: The later clause is רבי עקיבא, so the first clause is not
steps.stepSummary: A second point: the משנה names רבי עקיבא as disagreeing in the next clause, so the clause before it must belong to someone else.
steps.simpleTranslation: And furthermore: since the later clause is רבי עקיבא, the earlier clause is not רבי עקיבא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second, structural argument against רבי ינאי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a משנה brings רבי עקיבא's opinion only afterward, the clause before it is usually someone else's view. So the first clause should be the חכמים, not רבי עקיבא as רבי ינאי said.

keyTerms.meaning: And furthermore: introduces an additional argument.
The later clause of a משנה
The earlier (opening) clause of a משנה

phrases.english: And furthermore:
since the later clause is Rabbi Akiva,
the earlier clause is not Rabbi Akiva.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second challenge to the one in step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ינאי's attribution of the רישא to רבי עקיבא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה names רבי עקיבא only in the סיפא, which implies the רישא follows a different opinion.

steps.title: The whole משנה is רבי עקיבא, with missing words filled in
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the entire משנה follows רבי עקיבא and fills in missing words. Two separate עירובין permit both courtyards only when the inner courtyard built a small partition. Without it, רבי עקיבא forbids the outer courtyard because of the right of passage, and the חכמים disagree.
steps.simpleTranslation: The whole משנה is רבי עקיבא, and some words are missing. This is what it teaches: if each courtyard made its own עירוב, each is permitted by itself. When is this said? When the inner courtyard made a small partition. But if it did not make a partition, the outer courtyard is forbidden. These are the words of רבי עקיבא, who forbids the outer courtyard because the right of passage forbids. The חכמים say the right of passage does not forbid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers both challenges. It says the משנה is missing words, then rewrites it so that every part fits רבי עקיבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case of 'both permitted' was never a general rule. It applies only when a small partition separates the inner courtyard's passage. So it does not show that a permitted foot never forbids. Once the missing words are added, רבי עקיבא's name in the סיפא is explaining the clause right before it, so the רישא can also be his.

keyTerms.meaning: The whole of it (the entire משנה)
The text is missing words: a way to fill in a missing clause.
A small partition at the inner courtyard's opening
Right of passage: the inner residents' right to walk through the outer courtyard.
When is this said? (limits a ruling to a specific case)

steps.confusionAlert: The words 'דברי רבי עקיבא' here do not mean רבי עקיבא disagrees with the clause before them. In the fixed-up משנה, they explain that the clause itself is his.

phrases.english: The whole of it is Rabbi Akiva,
and it is missing words, and this is what it teaches:
if this one made an eiruv for itself and that one for itself —
this one is permitted by itself
and that one is permitted by itself.
When is this said?
When the inner courtyard made a small partition,
but if it did not make a small partition —
the outer one is forbidden; these are the words of Rabbi Akiva,
for Rabbi Akiva forbids the outer one,
because the right of passage forbids.
And the Sages say:
the right of passage does not forbid.

steps.triggerLanguage: כּוּלַּהּ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא הִיא, וְחַסּוֹרֵי מִיחַסְּרָא וְהָכִי קָתָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenges of steps 18 and 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Textual emendation (חסורי מחסרא): the משנה is rewritten so that every clause follows רבי עקיבא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The 'both permitted' clause is a general rule that a permitted foot does not forbid, so it must be the חכמים.
steps.terutzMaskana: The 'both permitted' clause is limited to a case with a small partition. Without one, רבי עקיבא forbids the outer courtyard, so the whole משנה is his and רבי ינאי stands.

steps.title: רב ביבי בר אביי challenges from the case of single residents
steps.stepSummary: From the משנה's line that courtyards of single residents need no עירוב, רב ביבי בר אביי infers that courtyards of many residents do. This again implies a permitted foot does not forbid but a forbidden foot does.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ביבי בר אביי objected: 'And if they belonged to single residents, they do not need to make an עירוב.' This implies that courtyards of many residents do need an עירוב. Apparently, a foot that is permitted in its own place does not forbid, but a forbidden foot does forbid!
steps.whatsHappening: A new challenge to רבי ינאי, this time from a different line of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With single residents, each courtyard is already permitted, so no עירוב is needed. With many residents, they need an עירוב only to make their own courtyard permitted. So the whole problem is a forbidden foot, and a permitted foot causes no problem. רבי עקיבא would not say this, so it seems to be the חכמים, which again goes against רבי ינאי.

keyTerms.meaning: Raises an objection from a source
Single residents (one person per courtyard)
Apparently, this shows that
In its own place

phrases.english: Rav Beivai bar Abaye objected:
"And if they belonged to single residents,
they do not need to make an eiruv."
This implies that those of many residents do need to make an eiruv;
apparently a foot permitted in its own place
does not forbid,
but a forbidden foot does forbid!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 20's answer, a new objection reopens the challenge to רבי ינאי.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ינאי's view (step 14) of how רבי עקיבא and the חכמים divide.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The single-resident clause implies that only a forbidden foot causes a problem. That is a view רבי עקיבא cannot hold, so the חכמים must hold that a forbidden foot forbids.

steps.title: רבינא challenges from the case of a resident who forgot
steps.stepSummary: רבינא cites a ruling: if a resident of the inner courtyard forgot to join the עירוב, both courtyards are forbidden. If no one forgot, both are permitted. So a permitted foot does not forbid, but a forbidden foot does.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבינא raised another objection: If one resident of the outer courtyard forgot and did not join the עירוב, the inner courtyard is permitted and the outer is forbidden. If one resident of the inner courtyard forgot and did not join the עירוב, both are forbidden. The reason is that he forgot. But if he did not forget, both are permitted. Apparently, a permitted foot does not forbid, but a forbidden foot does forbid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings one more challenge to רבי ינאי, built the same way as the previous one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the inner courtyard is forbidden because someone forgot, its residents' passage forbids the outer courtyard too. When no one forgot, both courtyards are permitted, so the inner residents' passage does no harm. This 'only a forbidden foot forbids' view cannot be רבי עקיבא, so the חכמים must agree a forbidden foot forbids, against רבי ינאי.

keyTerms.meaning: Forgot (to join the עירוב)
The inner courtyard
The outer courtyard
The reason is because: sets up an inference from the opposite case.

steps.whatToRemember: Three sources (steps 18, 21, 22) all point to one view: a permitted foot does not forbid, but a forbidden foot does. Since רבי עקיבא forbids even with a permitted foot, this seems to be the חכמים. That puts heavy pressure on רבי ינאי's claim that for the חכמים neither foot forbids.

phrases.english: And Ravina raised another objection:

phrases.aramaic: שָׁכַח אֶחָד מִן הַחִיצוֹנָה וְלֹא עֵירַב —
phrases.english: If one from the outer courtyard forgot and did not join the eiruv —
the inner one is permitted and the outer one is forbidden.

phrases.aramaic: שָׁכַח אֶחָד מִן הַפְּנִימִית וְלֹא עֵירַב —
phrases.english: If one from the inner courtyard forgot and did not join the eiruv —
both are forbidden.
The reason is that he forgot;
but if he did not forget, both are permitted.
Apparently a permitted foot does not forbid,
but a forbidden foot does forbid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A further objection with the same logic as step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ינאי's claim that the חכמים hold even a forbidden foot does not forbid.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The 'forgot' ruling shows a forbidden foot forbids while a permitted foot does not. רבי עקיבא cannot hold this, so it must be the חכמים, which contradicts רבי ינאי.

steps.title: רבין's corrected version: three separate opinions
steps.stepSummary: רבין reports that רבי ינאי actually taught a three-way dispute. The תנא קמא says a permitted foot does not forbid but a forbidden foot does. רבי עקיבא says even a permitted foot forbids. The later רבנן say neither foot forbids.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, when רבין came, he said in the name of רבי ינאי: there are three opinions on this matter. The first תנא holds that a permitted foot does not forbid, but a forbidden foot does forbid. רבי עקיבא holds that even a permitted foot forbids. The later רבנן hold that just as a permitted foot does not forbid, so too a forbidden foot does not forbid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the earlier version of רבי ינאי that kept running into challenges. It replaces it with רבין's version, which lays out three distinct opinions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier challenges kept showing that clauses of the משנה assume a middle view: a permitted foot does not forbid, but a forbidden foot does. The earlier version of רבי ינאי had no room for that view. Now the middle view gets its own owner, the תנא קמא. רבי עקיבא is the strictest, and the later רבנן are the most lenient, so every clause fits.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather; signals that the previous version is rejected
When רבין came (from ארץ ישראל to בבל); introduces a different reported version
Three disputing opinions
The 'foot' of someone permitted to carry in his own courtyard
The 'foot' of someone forbidden to carry in his own courtyard (e.g., his courtyard lacks a valid עירוב)
The later רבנן, who disagree with רבי עקיבא in the משנה

steps.whatToRemember: Three views: תנא קמא says only a forbidden foot forbids. רבי עקיבא says even a permitted foot forbids. The later רבנן say no foot forbids.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two groups of 'Rabbis.' The תנא קמא (the first, unnamed opinion) holds the middle view. The 'רבנן בתראי' (the later Rabbis, who argue with רבי עקיבא) hold the most lenient view. They are two different opinions.
steps.whyThisMatters: This three-way map is the key to reading the whole משנה. Each clause can now be assigned to the correct opinion without contradiction.

phrases.english: Rather, when Ravin came
phrases.notes: The גמרא drops the earlier version and goes with Ravin's report instead.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yannai said:
There are three disputes on this matter:
The first tanna holds:
a permitted foot does not forbid,
a forbidden foot does forbid.
phrases.notes: This is the middle view of the three.

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva holds:
even a permitted foot forbids.
And the later Rabbis hold:
just as a permitted foot does not forbid —
so too a forbidden foot does not forbid.
phrases.notes: This is the most lenient view.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא כִּי אֲתָא רָבִין אָמַר רַבִּי יַנַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the run of challenges (steps 18–22) by replacing the earlier version of רבי ינאי with a corrected one.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Corrected version of the אמורא's statement (a different report of the tradition)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי ינאי recognized only two positions, so the middle view found in the sources had no owner.
steps.terutzMaskana: There are three positions. The middle view (a permitted foot does not forbid, a forbidden foot does) belongs to the תנא קמא, so all the sources fit.

steps.title: What does 'one place' mean in the משנה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next clause of the משנה, about placing the עירוב in one place when someone forgot to contribute, and asks what 'one place' means.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'If they placed their עירוב in one place, and one person forgot, whether from the inner courtyard, etc.' What is meant by 'one place'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to a new line of the משנה and asks what the phrase 'one place' refers to. This sets up the explanation that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה rules that if one person forgot to join, both courtyards are forbidden. The גמרא wants to know exactly where this shared עירוב was placed. Where the עירוב sits may decide whether the inner courtyard can separate itself from the outer one.

keyTerms.meaning: They placed their עירוב (the shared food that joins the residents)
One place
Forgot (to contribute to the עירוב)
The inner courtyard, whose residents pass through the outer one
Etc.; the rest of the quote is understood

phrases.english: If they placed their eiruv in one place
phrases.notes: This is a quote from the משנה.

phrases.aramaic: וְשָׁכַח אֶחָד בֵּין מִן הַפְּנִימִית וְכוּ׳.
phrases.english: and one person forgot, whether from the inner courtyard, etc.
What is meant by 'one place'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the 'foot' dispute and opens a new topic: the meaning of a phrase in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which location the משנה means by 'one place' where both courtyards' עירוב was put.

steps.title: A memory aid for the coming discussion
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a סימן, a string of key words that helps the learner remember the order of the statements that follow.
steps.simpleTranslation: (A memory aid: outer; itself; in the house of a single resident; רבינא; where the inner one did not forget.)
steps.whatsHappening: This is not an argument. It is a list of keywords, one for each statement coming next, so the learner can remember their order. It sets up the discussion that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word points to an upcoming statement. 'Outer' points to רב יהודה's explanation. The other words point to later teachings, including one by רבינא and a case where no one from the inner courtyard forgot. The list adds no new law.

keyTerms.meaning: Mnemonic; a memory aid listing upcoming statements
The outer courtyard
The house of a single resident

steps.confusionAlert: Don't try to read the סימן as a sentence with meaning. It is only a list of hint-words for the statements that come next.

phrases.english: (Mnemonic: Outer; itself;
in the house of a single resident; Ravina;
where the inner one did not forget)

steps.alternativePossibleLabel: Mnemonic / structural setup (סימן), not a true argumentative step
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Pauses before the answer to the question in step 24 and lists the upcoming statements.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling; a memory aid only.

steps.title: 'One place' means the outer courtyard
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of רב says 'one place' is the outer courtyard. It is called 'אחד' because it is a place 'מיוחד', meaning set aside, for the residents of both courtyards.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: it means the outer courtyard. Why did they call it 'one place'? Because it is a place set aside for both of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 24. The 'one place' in the משנה is the outer courtyard, and the word 'אחד' hints at 'מיוחד', meaning designated for both groups.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The residents of the inner courtyard walk through the outer one, so the outer courtyard serves both groups. If their עירוב sits there, the inner residents are tied to the outer courtyard and cannot separate from it. So if someone in the outer courtyard forgot to join, the inner courtyard is forbidden too. If the עירוב had been placed in the inner courtyard, the inner residents could separate themselves and carry in their own courtyard.

keyTerms.meaning: רב יהודה reporting a teaching of his teacher רב
They called it
Designated, set aside; a wordplay on אֶחָד
For both of them (the residents of both courtyards)

steps.whatToRemember: 'One place' = the outer courtyard. It is called 'אחד' because it is 'מיוחד', set aside for both courtyards. Since the shared עירוב is there, the inner courtyard cannot separate itself from the outer one.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why, under the משנה's ruling, even the inner courtyard becomes forbidden when someone from the outer courtyard forgot to join. The location of the עירוב is what ties the two courtyards together.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
The outer courtyard.
phrases.notes: This answers the question of what 'one place' means.

phrases.english: And why did they call it 'one place'?
Because it is a place designated for both of them.
phrases.notes: There's a play on words here: אֶחָד (one) hints at מְיוּחָד (designated).

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב חִיצוֹנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'One place' is the outer courtyard, called 'אחד' because it is 'מיוחד', designated for the residents of both courtyards.
